lessons.title: Turn prospect research into a personalized cold outreach message with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a handful of real facts about a prospect into a short, specific cold email and LinkedIn message that doesn't read like a mail-merge.
lessons.goal: Draft a personalized cold outreach email and LinkedIn message from real prospect research notes, with no invented facts about the prospect or their company.
lessons.whyItMatters: Buyers can spot a mail-merge cold email in one sentence, and a generic opener kills the message before the pitch even starts. Prospects respond to outreach that shows you actually looked at their company and role, but writing a genuinely personalized note for every name on a list is exactly the step reps skip when the list is long. A prompt that turns a few real research notes into a tight, specific opener lets you personalize at the volume your pipeline actually needs.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a Claude account open. Spend 5-10 minutes researching the prospect first (LinkedIn profile, company site, recent news) and write down 3-5 real facts. This lesson turns research into a message — it doesn't do the research for you.
steps: Open a new chat in Claude.
Paste your researched facts: the prospect's role, company, and something specific and current — a launch, a hire, a stated priority, a post they wrote.
Add what you sell in one sentence and the single problem it solves that's most likely relevant to them.
Use the outreach prompt below, which bans generic personalization phrases and invented facts.
Ask for two short variants — an email and a LinkedIn message — so both channels are ready.
Read both against your notes and cut anything that isn't traceable to a fact you supplied.
Send from your own email or LinkedIn account.
lessons.prompt:
I'm writing cold outreach to a prospect. Use only the facts I give you below — do not invent details about their company, role, achievements, or priorities that I haven't stated.

Prospect: [NAME, TITLE, COMPANY]
Researched facts (use these for personalization): [PASTE 3-5 REAL FACTS, e.g. a recent funding round, a role change, a post they wrote, a product they launched, a stated company priority]
What I sell: [PRODUCT/SERVICE IN ONE SENTENCE]
Problem it solves that's likely relevant to them: [ONE SENTENCE]
My ask: [e.g., a 15-minute call, a reply with interest, a resource to send]

Rules:
- Open with a specific, genuine reference to ONE researched fact — not a generic compliment ("I saw your company is growing!") or a fake-personal opener ("I noticed we're both in the same industry").
- Do not use hype words like "revolutionary," "game-changing," or "synergy."
- Keep the email under 100 words. Keep the LinkedIn message under 60 words.
- One clear, low-friction ask — not multiple options.
- No fake urgency ("limited spots," "only reaching out to a few companies").

Write:
1. A subject line under 6 words.
2. The email version.
3. A shorter LinkedIn message version.
lessons.explanation: Requiring the opener to reference one specific researched fact, rather than a generic compliment, is what separates this from a templated blast — it forces the model to use the one piece of real information you gave it instead of filling the opening line with filler. Banning hype words and fake urgency keeps the tone credible, since both are reliable tells of a mass email. Capping word count and limiting the message to a single ask matches how a busy prospect actually reads a cold message — fast, and looking for a reason to stop.
lessons.example:
Facts: Dana Reyes, VP of Ops at a 40-person logistics startup, posted on LinkedIn last week about struggling to onboard new warehouse staff fast enough for peak season. Product: a training-checklist automation tool. Problem it solves: cuts new-hire ramp time. Ask: a 15-minute call.

Expected output: an email opening with something like "Saw your post last week about onboarding speed heading into peak season" rather than a generic greeting, naming the ramp-time problem in one line, and closing with a single ask for a 15-minute call — with a shorter LinkedIn variant under 60 words making the same point more tersely.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, research one real prospect for 5-10 minutes, gather 3-5 real facts, and generate both message versions with this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: A specific, non-generic email and LinkedIn message under the word limits, with every personalized detail traceable to a fact you actually researched.
commonMistakes: Handing over vague research ("they seem successful") instead of a specific, current fact to open with.
Letting the model's opener slide into a generic compliment when the real fact feels thin.
Including more than one ask, which makes the message harder to reply to quickly.
Reusing the same opener structure for every prospect, which starts to read as formulaic even when the facts differ.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running list of 3-5 fact bullets per prospect as you research, before you ever open Claude — separating research from writing keeps each step faster and the guardrail easier to check.

lessons.title: Write a follow-up sequence that doesn't feel robotic with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn one unanswered outreach message into a 3-4 touch follow-up sequence where each message adds a new angle instead of repeating "just checking in."
lessons.goal: Produce a 3-4 message follow-up sequence for a prospect who hasn't replied, where each touch has a distinct angle instead of restating the same ask.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most follow-ups fail because they're the first email again with "just following up!" tacked on, which reads as pressure rather than value. Prospects who eventually buy often need several touches, but each one needs its own reason to earn a reply — a new angle, a useful resource, a specific question, a graceful exit. Planning the whole sequence at once, instead of writing each email in isolation right before sending it, is what keeps the touches from blurring into repeats of each other.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your original outreach message (or a short summary of what you sent) ready, plus anything you know about the prospect's likely situation — busy season, wrong timing, no signal at all.
steps: Open a new chat in ChatGPT.
Paste your original message and note how many days it's been since you sent it.
Use the sequence prompt below, specifying the channel and number of touches.
Ask for each message to use a different angle: added value, a specific question, social proof, and a low-pressure break-up message.
Check that no message repeats the previous one's wording or restates the same ask verbatim.
Space the sends according to the suggested cadence rather than sending them all close together.
Stop the sequence the moment you get any reply, including a "not now."
lessons.prompt:
Write a follow-up sequence for a prospect who hasn't replied to my outreach.

Original message I sent: [PASTE ORIGINAL MESSAGE]
Days since I sent it: [NUMBER]
What I know about their likely situation: [e.g., busy quarter, no signal either way, said "maybe later"]
Channel: [email / LinkedIn]
Number of follow-ups: [3 or 4]

Rules:
- Do not repeat "just checking in," "following up," "circling back," or restate the original ask word-for-word in any message.
- Each message must use a different angle: (1) add one new piece of value — a relevant insight, resource, or question, not asked before; (2) ask one specific, low-effort question; (3) offer light social proof or a relevant example, only if I provide one — do not invent a client name or result; (4) a short, no-pressure "break-up" message that makes it easy for them to say not now.
- Keep each message under 60 words.
- Suggest a sending cadence (days between each message).
- Do not invent case studies, statistics, or client names — use [YOUR EXAMPLE] as a placeholder if I don't supply one.
lessons.explanation: Naming the exact phrases to avoid ("just checking in," "circling back") stops the model from defaulting to the filler openers that make follow-ups feel automated, and assigning each touch a distinct required angle forces genuine variation instead of four versions of the same email. Explicitly banning invented case studies or client names matters here because "social proof" is one of the categories a model will happily fabricate if you don't constrain it. Including a break-up message as the final touch is what keeps the sequence from feeling like pressure that never lets up — it gives the prospect a graceful, low-stakes way to opt out.
lessons.example:
Original message: a cold email pitching a scheduling tool to an operations manager, sent 6 days ago with no reply. Channel: email, 4 touches.

Expected output: touch 1 adds a new angle (e.g., a specific way the tool handles a common ops pain point not mentioned before); touch 2 asks one direct, low-effort question ("Is scheduling handled centrally or per-team at your company?"); touch 3 offers proof only if the rep supplied a real example, otherwise uses the [YOUR EXAMPLE] placeholder; touch 4 is a short break-up message like "I'll leave it here for now — reply anytime if priorities shift." A suggested cadence of roughly 3-4 days between touches should be included.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, use a real unanswered outreach message from your pipeline to generate a 4-touch sequence with this prompt, then schedule the sends at the suggested cadence.
lessons.expectedResult: A 3-4 message sequence where each message reads distinctly from the others, none open with generic filler, and the final message gives the prospect an easy, pressure-free way to disengage.
commonMistakes: Sending all the follow-ups on a fixed schedule regardless of the suggested cadence or the prospect's context.
Letting the model invent a client result or statistic for the social-proof touch instead of using a real one or a placeholder.
Continuing the sequence after a "not interested" or "maybe later" reply instead of stopping it.
Reusing the exact same sequence wording for every prospect without swapping in their specific context.
lessons.proTip: Keep one durable break-up-message template you like and reuse the exact wording every time — it's the message where personalization matters least and consistency signals professionalism most.

lessons.title: Turn your real sales objections into response scripts with Claude
lessons.summary: Feed Claude the actual objections you hear on calls and get honest, practiced response options grounded in what your product really does.
lessons.goal: Build a set of response scripts for the specific objections you actually hear from prospects, grounded in your product's real strengths and honest about its real limitations.
lessons.whyItMatters: Objections happen live, with no time to think, and generic scripts from a training deck rarely match what you actually sell or what your prospects actually say. Building scripts from your own logged objections — and being honest about where your product falls short rather than deflecting — is what makes responses sound like you instead of a sales-training cliché, and it protects you from overpromising something you'll have to walk back later.
steps: Write down the objection in the prospect's actual words, not a paraphrase.
List your product's real, honest strengths relevant to that objection, and any real limitation you shouldn't dodge.
Use the objection prompt to get 2-3 response approaches, not one script.
Ask for the reasoning behind each approach so you know when to use which.
Have Claude roleplay the prospect pushing back further so you can practice out loud.
Adjust the wording to your own voice — don't memorize anything verbatim.
Save the approaches that actually worked on real calls as your personal playbook.
lessons.prompt:
Help me prepare responses to a real sales objection.

Objection, in the prospect's own words: [PASTE EXACT OBJECTION]
What I'm selling: [PRODUCT/SERVICE]
Real strengths relevant to this objection: [LIST — only things that are actually true]
Real limitations I shouldn't dodge: [LIST, if any — e.g., "we don't integrate with X yet," "we're pricier than the low-end competitor"]

Rules:
- Do not invent features, integrations, pricing, or claims about my product that I haven't told you are true.
- If a limitation exists, at least one response approach should acknowledge it honestly rather than talking around it.
- Give 2-3 different response approaches (e.g., reframe-the-cost, evidence-led, acknowledge-and-pivot), each 3-5 sentences of talking points, not a script to read verbatim.
- Add a one-line note on when each approach fits best.
- Then roleplay the prospect pushing back harder on my strongest approach so I can practice responding out loud.
lessons.explanation: Asking for talking points instead of a verbatim script keeps the output usable when a live conversation goes off-script, since a memorized line falls apart the moment the prospect responds unpredictably. Requiring at least one approach to acknowledge a real limitation honestly, rather than deflecting, is the guardrail that keeps this from turning into overpromising — prospects tend to trust a rep more after an honest "here's what we don't do yet" than after a dodge they can later disprove. The roleplay step is what turns this into practice rather than a reading exercise, and banning invented features or pricing keeps you from rehearsing a claim you can't actually back up on the real call.
lessons.example:
Objection, verbatim: "Your pricing is almost double what [competitor] charges." Strengths: dedicated onboarding support, a feature the competitor lacks that directly addresses the prospect's stated pain point. Limitation: yes, list price is genuinely higher.

Expected output: a reframe-the-cost approach connecting the price gap to the specific feature and onboarding support; an acknowledge-and-pivot approach that admits the price difference honestly before pivoting to total cost of ownership or time saved; guidance on which fits a price-sensitive versus a value-focused buyer; then a roleplay where the model pushes back with "but that's still $X more a year" so the rep can practice responding.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take one objection you've heard on a real call this month and run it through this prompt, then do the roleplay step out loud at least once before your next call.
lessons.expectedResult: Two or three honest, deal-usable response approaches you can adapt in your own words, plus at least one round of practiced pushback before you face the objection live again.
commonMistakes: Letting Claude invent a feature or integration to answer an objection instead of sticking to what's actually true.
Memorizing a response word-for-word, which sounds scripted and brittle when the prospect answers differently than expected.
Skipping the honest-limitation approach in favor of only the most flattering framing.
Skipping the roleplay and only reading the talking points silently.
lessons.proTip: Log the exact wording of every real objection you hear for a month — the patterns that show up three or more times are the ones worth building a permanent script for.

lessons.title: Draft a proposal and quote from discovery call notes with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn messy discovery call notes into a structured proposal draft — problem, solution, scope, and next steps — without inventing pricing or promises that weren't discussed.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured proposal draft from real discovery notes, with pricing and scope left as clearly marked placeholders unless you supply real figures.
lessons.whyItMatters: Proposals sent within a day or two of a strong discovery call close at a meaningfully higher rate than ones that arrive a week later, but writing a tailored proposal from scratch every time is slow enough that momentum gets lost. The risk with letting AI speed this up is scope and pricing errors — a proposal that promises a deliverable never discussed, or states a price you never quoted, is a credibility problem at best and a contract dispute at worst. A tight prompt turns real notes into a fast draft while keeping pricing and scope strictly to what was actually said.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your raw discovery call notes ready — the prospect's stated problem, goals, budget signals if any, and what was actually discussed as in-scope.
steps: Gather your discovery notes: stated problem, goals, timeline, any budget signal, and what was discussed as in-scope.
Use the proposal prompt below, which restricts scope and pricing to what you provide.
Leave pricing as a placeholder if it wasn't explicitly discussed on the call.
Review the "Scope items to confirm" list the prompt generates and check each one against your notes.
Fill in real pricing yourself before sending — never let the model estimate it.
Ask for a shorter executive-summary version to lead the document.
Send from your own proposal or document tool after a final read-through.
lessons.prompt:
Draft a sales proposal from my discovery call notes. Use only what's in the notes — do not invent scope items, deliverables, timelines, or pricing that weren't discussed.

Prospect / company: [NAME]
Discovery notes (problem, goals, timeline, budget signals, what was discussed as in-scope): [PASTE RAW NOTES]
What we sell / our solution: [SHORT DESCRIPTION]

Structure the proposal as:
1. Executive summary (3-4 sentences, restating their problem in their own terms)
2. Problem statement (grounded only in what they told you)
3. Proposed solution and how it addresses each stated problem
4. Scope of work — list only items explicitly discussed; for anything you're inferring rather than quoting from the notes, put it under a separate "Scope items to confirm" section instead of the main scope
5. Pricing — use [PRICE PLACEHOLDER] unless I've given you an actual number; never estimate a number yourself
6. Timeline and next steps

Tone: confident, consultative, no filler adjectives like "cutting-edge" or "best-in-class."
lessons.explanation: Separating confirmed scope from inferred scope into two distinct sections is the core guardrail — it's the difference between a proposal you can send as-is after a quick check and one where a promised deliverable silently slipped in from the model's own inference. Forcing pricing to stay a placeholder unless you explicitly supply a number prevents the single most costly kind of error a proposal can contain. Leading with an executive summary that restates the prospect's problem in their own terms is what makes a proposal feel consultative rather than templated, since it shows the document was built from their actual call, not a boilerplate structure.
lessons.example:
Notes: prospect's operations team spends roughly 6 hours a week manually reconciling shipment data across two systems; they want it down to under an hour; timeline mentioned was "before end of quarter"; no price was discussed on the call.

Expected output: an executive summary naming the 6-hour reconciliation burden and the under-one-hour goal in their words; a scope section listing only the reconciliation automation discussed; anything like "reporting dashboard" that wasn't explicitly mentioned goes under "Scope items to confirm" rather than the main scope; the pricing section shows [PRICE PLACEHOLDER] rather than any invented figure; the timeline section reflects the stated end-of-quarter target.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, take notes from a real recent discovery call and generate a proposal draft with this prompt, then fill in real pricing yourself before it goes anywhere near a prospect.
lessons.expectedResult: A structured, consultative proposal draft with confirmed scope clearly separated from anything inferred, and no pricing figure that didn't come directly from you.
commonMistakes: Letting an inferred deliverable stay in the main scope section instead of moving it to "to confirm."
Accepting a placeholder pricing section without replacing it with real numbers before sending.
Pasting thin or vague discovery notes and expecting a specific, tailored proposal back.
Skipping the final read-through against the original call notes before sending.
lessons.proTip: Take discovery notes in the same structure every time — problem, goals, timeline, budget signal, in-scope items — and this becomes a 10-minute draft instead of a from-scratch write-up for every deal.

lessons.title: Research a prospect and their company before a call with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Get a cited briefing on a company and prospect ahead of a discovery or sales call — recent news, funding, leadership moves, likely priorities — with sources you can verify.
lessons.goal: Produce a cited pre-call briefing on a prospect's company that surfaces recent, relevant, verifiable context, prepared ahead of the call rather than guessed at cold.
lessons.whyItMatters: Showing up to a call with real, current context changes the entire tone of the conversation — prospects notice immediately when a rep clearly hasn't looked them up. Manually checking a company site, LinkedIn, news, and funding databases for every call is slow enough that reps skip it under a packed calendar. ChatGPT's Deep Research mode browses many sources and returns a cited report, so the briefing comes with a citation trail you can spot-check before you rely on any of it in the room — run it early enough before the call, since it takes several minutes rather than seconds.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a ChatGPT Plus account or higher — Deep Research isn't available on the Free or Go tiers. Plus includes about 10 Deep Research runs per month, so save them for calls that matter.
steps: Open ChatGPT and select Deep Research in the composer rather than a normal chat, so it runs genuine multi-step web research.
Name the exact company and prospect, plus what kind of call this is (discovery, demo, renewal).
Answer any clarifying questions ChatGPT asks before it starts researching — this shapes what it actually looks for.
Start this early enough before the call — Deep Research typically takes several minutes to longer, so run it while you finish other prep, not in the two minutes right before you dial in.
Ask specifically for recent news, funding or leadership changes, and anything suggesting a current priority relevant to what you sell.
Click through 2-3 of the citations yourself to confirm they're recent and accurate before the call.
Ask a follow-up narrowing to the prospect's specific role or team if the first pass was company-wide.
Note the date you ran the research — company context changes fast, so re-run it if the call slips by more than a week or two.
lessons.prompt:
Research [COMPANY NAME] and, if publicly findable, [PROSPECT NAME, TITLE] ahead of a [discovery / demo / renewal] call.

I need, with a source and date for each:
1. Any news from the last 3-6 months (funding, leadership changes, layoffs, product launches, expansion)
2. The prospect's role and how long they've been in it, if publicly available
3. Anything publicly stated (press, company blog, the prospect's own posts) that suggests a current priority relevant to [WHAT I SELL, ONE SENTENCE]
4. Basic company facts: size, industry, and any competitors they're commonly compared to

Cite each item with its source and publish date. Flag clearly if you couldn't find prospect-specific or recent-enough information rather than filling the gap with general or outdated context.
lessons.explanation: Naming both the company and, where public, the specific prospect is what pushes Deep Research toward genuinely relevant results instead of generic company-overview content you could get from any search. Requiring a source and date on every item gives you a citation trail to sanity-check before the call, rather than repeating something stale or wrong to the prospect's face. The explicit instruction to flag missing information, rather than quietly filling gaps with older or generic context, is what keeps this from producing a confident-sounding briefing built on outdated facts — and because Deep Research genuinely browses the web over several minutes rather than answering from memory, that citation trail is real and checkable.
lessons.example: Query scoped to a mid-size logistics company and its VP of Operations ahead of a discovery call should return cited items such as a recent funding round or leadership hire, the VP's tenure in the role if public, a company blog post or press mention suggesting an operational priority relevant to a scheduling tool, and basic size/industry facts — each with a linked, dated source, and a clear note if the prospect-specific information wasn't found.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account (Plus or higher), run this as a Deep Research brief ahead of your next real sales call, giving yourself enough lead time for it to finish, and click through at least two citations to confirm they're accurate before you get on the call.
lessons.expectedResult: A cited pre-call briefing with at least one specific, current, verifiable detail you can naturally reference on the call, and a clear flag for anything the search couldn't confirm.
commonMistakes: Starting the research two minutes before the call instead of leaving enough time for Deep Research to actually finish browsing.
Referencing a fact on the call without having opened its citation to confirm it's current and accurate.
Running the research too far in advance and not re-checking it if the call gets rescheduled.
Asking a question broad enough to return generic company-overview content instead of anything role- or priority-specific.
lessons.proTip: Create a ChatGPT Project for your sales research with this prompt saved as a project instruction — Projects now integrate Deep Research directly, so every new research run in that project starts from the same standing instructions instead of a blank composer.

lessons.title: Build a reusable sales messaging library with Claude Projects
lessons.summary: Turn your best value props, objection responses, and proof points into a standing Claude Project so every future outreach, follow-up, or proposal draft starts from consistent, pre-approved messaging instead of a blank page.
lessons.goal: Set up a Claude Project containing your team's real messaging assets and standing rules, so any future prompt for outreach, follow-ups, or objections stays consistent without re-explaining context every time.
lessons.whyItMatters: The earlier lessons in this path work prompt by prompt, but every fresh chat starts from zero — you retype the same guardrails, re-paste the same value props, and tone quietly drifts between reps or between your own good days and rushed ones. A standing project loaded with your actual proof points, approved claims, and tone rules turns every future request into a two-line ask, and keeps every rep on a team pulling from the same source of truth instead of individually-remembered talking points.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Requires a Claude plan with Projects. Gather your real messaging assets first: your best-performing value props, 2-3 real proof points or case studies you're allowed to cite, your standard objection responses, and any tone or compliance rules your team follows.
steps: Create a new Claude Project named for your messaging library (e.g., "Sales Messaging — [Product/Team]").
Write custom instructions for the project stating the standing rules: never invent pricing, features, or client names; always flag inferred versus confirmed claims; match a defined tone.
Upload your real assets as project knowledge: approved value props, real proof points, objection-response notes, and any compliance-sensitive language to avoid.
Test it with a fresh request — a new cold outreach draft — and check whether it pulled from your uploaded assets instead of generating generic messaging.
Refine the custom instructions based on what came out wrong the first time (tone too stiff, a claim that needed a caveat, etc.).
Use the project for every future outreach, follow-up, objection, or proposal prompt instead of starting a plain new chat.
Review and update the uploaded assets quarterly as proof points, pricing, or positioning change.
lessons.prompt:
Project custom instructions:

You are helping me write sales messaging — cold outreach, follow-ups, objection responses, and proposal drafts. Follow these standing rules on every request in this project:

1. Only use claims, proof points, client examples, and pricing that appear in the uploaded project knowledge or that I state directly in the chat. Never invent a statistic, client name, feature, or price.
2. If a request needs a fact not in the uploaded knowledge, say so and ask for it or use a clearly marked placeholder — do not fill the gap yourself.
3. Default tone: [DESCRIBE YOUR TEAM'S TONE, e.g., "direct, consultative, no hype adjectives like 'revolutionary' or 'game-changing'"].
4. Keep cold outreach under 100 words, follow-ups under 60 words, unless I specify otherwise.
5. When drafting an objection response, always offer at least one option that acknowledges a real limitation honestly rather than only flattering framings.

Uploaded knowledge should include: approved value props, 2-3 real proof points/case studies, standard objection responses, and any compliance or legal language restrictions.

For each new request in this project, I'll just give you the prospect/situation details — you should pull tone and claims from the standing rules and uploaded knowledge automatically.
lessons.explanation: Putting the anti-invention and placeholder rules into the project's standing instructions, rather than repeating them in every single prompt, is what makes this scale — the guardrails apply automatically to every future request instead of depending on you remembering to add them. Uploading real proof points and objection responses as project knowledge, rather than pasting them into chat each time, is what lets a two-line prompt still produce a specific, on-brand draft instead of a generic one. Requiring an honest-limitation option in objection responses, as a standing rule rather than a one-off request, keeps the whole library credible instead of just persuasive.
lessons.example: After setup, a rep types only: "Cold outreach to a VP of Sales at a 200-person SaaS company, they just posted about missing quota targets this quarter." Expected output: a sub-100-word email that references the quota post specifically, pulls a relevant value prop and proof point from the uploaded knowledge rather than a generic one, matches the defined tone, and doesn't need the rep to re-paste any guardrails — because the project's standing instructions already enforce them.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, create this project, upload your real messaging assets, and run one full test request for a live prospect to confirm the output pulls from your uploaded knowledge rather than generic language.
lessons.expectedResult: A working Claude Project that produces consistent, on-brand, fact-grounded sales messaging from short prompts, without you re-explaining tone or re-pasting proof points each time.
commonMistakes: Uploading stale proof points or pricing and forgetting to refresh them as the business changes.
Writing standing instructions so vague ("be professional") that they don't actually constrain tone or claims.
Never testing the project with a real request before relying on it for a live prospect.
Letting every rep on a team maintain their own separate project instead of sharing one source of truth for approved claims.
lessons.proTip: Schedule a recurring quarterly review of the uploaded knowledge — pricing, proof points, and positioning drift faster than most teams remember to update a reference document.

lessons.title: Write a job description that attracts the right candidates with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn rough role requirements into a clear, inclusive job description that filters for the right candidates instead of flooding you with mismatched applicants.
lessons.goal: Produce a clear, inclusive job description from your real role requirements, with no invented responsibilities, benefits, or requirements, and any exclusionary language flagged.
lessons.whyItMatters: The job description is the first filter in your entire hiring funnel — a vague or bloated one gets flooded with mismatched applicants, while language that's unintentionally coded toward a certain age, gender, or background quietly suppresses qualified candidates who'd otherwise apply. Writing a strong JD from a rough list of requirements is fast with AI, but only if it stays grounded in what the role actually needs and actively flags language worth reconsidering, rather than defaulting to generic corporate phrasing that describes no role in particular.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Gather your real role details: the actual responsibilities, required and preferred qualifications, reporting line, and any confirmed compensation or benefits info you're allowed to publish.
steps: Open a new chat in Claude.
Paste your rough role notes: responsibilities, must-have and nice-to-have qualifications, reporting structure.
Use the job description prompt below, which restricts content to what you provide and flags exclusionary language.
Review the "Language flagged for review" section and decide whether to change each flagged item.
Confirm the requirements list actually reflects must-haves versus nice-to-haves — cut anything that's really just a preference dressed up as a requirement.
Add compensation information only if your company is ready to publish it.
Post the version you've reviewed, not the raw first draft.
lessons.prompt:
Write a job description using only the details I provide below. Do not invent responsibilities, qualifications, benefits, or company details I haven't stated.

Role title: [TITLE]
Reporting line: [WHO THEY REPORT TO]
Real responsibilities: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES]
Must-have qualifications: [LIST]
Nice-to-have qualifications: [LIST]
Compensation/benefits I can publish: [LIST, or "not publishing"]
Company/team context: [1-2 SENTENCES]

Rules:
- Clearly separate "Required" from "Preferred" qualifications — do not blend them.
- Avoid gendered, age-coded, or unnecessarily exclusionary language (e.g., "young and energetic," "digital native," "culture fit" used vaguely, unnecessary degree requirements for roles that don't need them). Flag anything in my notes that reads this way in a separate "Language flagged for review" section, rather than silently rewriting it.
- Do not add generic corporate filler ("fast-paced environment," "wear many hats") unless it reflects something I actually described.
- Keep the required qualifications list to what's genuinely necessary to do the job, not an aspirational wish list.

Output the JD, then the "Language flagged for review" section separately.
lessons.explanation: Separating required from preferred qualifications is the single change that most affects who applies — bundling a long wish list into "requirements" is a well-documented reason qualified candidates, especially from underrepresented groups, self-select out. Asking the model to flag exclusionary language in a separate section, rather than silently rewriting your notes, keeps you in control of the final wording while still surfacing patterns you might not catch yourself. Banning generic filler phrases forces the JD to actually describe this role rather than reading like every other listing on the same job board.
lessons.example:
Notes: a mid-level data analyst role reporting to the analytics manager, responsibilities include building recurring reports and ad hoc analysis, requirements originally drafted as "bachelor's degree required, 3+ years experience, young and energetic team player."

Expected output: a JD with a clear Required list (e.g., 3+ years relevant analysis experience) separated from Preferred, and a "Language flagged for review" section noting that "young and energetic" reads as age-coded and that a bachelor's degree requirement may be worth reconsidering if the role doesn't genuinely need one — left for the hiring manager to decide, not silently removed.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, draft a JD for a real open (or upcoming) role using this prompt, and make an explicit decision on every item in the flagged-language section before posting.
lessons.expectedResult: A clear, role-specific job description with required and preferred qualifications genuinely separated, and a reviewed decision on every flagged language item before it goes live.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the flagged-language section instead of making an active decision on each item.
Letting an aspirational wish list stay in "Required," which discourages qualified candidates from applying.
Publishing generic filler phrases that don't reflect the actual role, making the posting forgettable among competitors.
Adding compensation details that aren't yet approved for public posting.
lessons.proTip: Run your three most recent job descriptions through the flagged-language check even if you're not rewriting them — patterns you don't notice in one posting often show up clearly once several are compared.

lessons.title: Build an interview question set for a role and competency with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Generate a structured interview question set organized by the specific competencies that matter for a role, with legally risky question types filtered out.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured, competency-based interview question set for a specific role, with follow-up probes and no questions that touch on protected characteristics.
lessons.whyItMatters: Ad hoc interview questions — improvised on the spot or reused from whatever the last hiring manager had on hand — lead to inconsistent evaluation across candidates and make it harder to compare them fairly afterward. Some improvised questions also stray into legally risky territory (age, family status, disability, national origin) without the interviewer realizing it. A structured, competency-based set that's checked for that risk up front gives every candidate a comparable interview and gives you a defensible record of why a hiring decision was made.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Know the role and the 3-5 competencies you're actually evaluating for (e.g., stakeholder communication, technical troubleshooting, prioritization under ambiguity) — this works best when you name real competencies, not just "good communicator."
steps: List the role and the 3-5 competencies this interview needs to evaluate.
Use the question-set prompt below.
Review every question for anything that could be read as touching age, family status, disability, religion, national origin, or other protected characteristics.
Ask for a follow-up probe question under each main question to use if the candidate's answer is thin.
Adjust or cut any question that doesn't map clearly to one of your named competencies.
Share the finalized set with every interviewer on the panel so everyone evaluates from the same structure.
lessons.prompt:
Build a structured interview question set for this role.

Role: [TITLE]
Competencies to evaluate (be specific): [LIST 3-5, e.g., "cross-functional stakeholder communication," "debugging under time pressure," "prioritizing conflicting deadlines"]
Interview format: [e.g., 45-minute behavioral interview / technical screen]

Rules:
- Group questions under each named competency — do not produce a generic, un-grouped list.
- Use a behavioral or situational format ("Tell me about a time..." / "How would you approach...") tied to real job scenarios, not abstract hypotheticals.
- For each main question, add one follow-up probe to use if the candidate's initial answer is vague.
- Do not include any question that touches on age, family or marital status, pregnancy, disability, religion, national origin, or similar protected characteristics, even indirectly (e.g., avoid "do you have reliable childcare" or "where are you originally from").
- Flag, in a separate note, any of my named competencies that are too vague to write a good question for, so I can sharpen them first.

Give 2-3 questions per competency.
lessons.explanation: Grouping questions explicitly by named competency, rather than producing one flat list, is what makes the set usable for structured evaluation afterward — you can score a candidate competency by competency instead of trying to reconstruct which question mapped to what. Naming the exact protected-characteristic categories to avoid is more reliable than a general "keep it appropriate" instruction, because indirect versions of these questions (childcare logistics, "where are you from") are the ones interviewers most often ask without realizing the risk. Requiring a follow-up probe under each question gives interviewers a next move when an answer is too vague to evaluate, instead of letting a weak answer pass unchallenged.
lessons.example:
Role: senior customer support lead. Competencies: de-escalating frustrated customers, coaching junior reps, prioritizing under a full queue.

Expected output: under "de-escalating frustrated customers," a question like "Tell me about a time you handled an angry customer who wanted a refund outside policy" with a follow-up probe ("What did you say first, and why?"); similar grouped sets for the other two competencies; no questions anywhere touching family status, age, or similar categories.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, build a question set for a role you're currently hiring for using its real competencies, and review every question yourself for protected-characteristic risk before using it.
lessons.expectedResult: A competency-grouped interview question set with follow-up probes, reviewed and confirmed free of legally risky question types, ready to share with the full interview panel.
commonMistakes: Naming vague competencies like "good team player" instead of something specific enough to write a real question for.
Skipping your own review of the flagged-risk instruction and trusting the output without checking it.
Using a different, improvised question set for different candidates in the same role, which breaks the ability to compare them fairly.
Treating the follow-up probe as optional instead of using it when an answer is genuinely thin.
lessons.proTip: Reuse the same competency-grouped question set for every candidate in a single hiring round — the consistency is what makes side-by-side comparison after the interviews actually fair.

lessons.title: Write candidate outreach messages that get replies with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a candidate's real profile details into a specific, personalized sourcing message instead of a generic "exciting opportunity" template.
lessons.goal: Draft a personalized outreach message to a passive candidate from real profile details, with no invented facts about their background or experience.
lessons.whyItMatters: Passive candidates get several generic recruiter messages a week and can tell within a sentence which ones were actually written about them. A message that references something specific and real from their background — a project, a role transition, a skill they've highlighted — gets meaningfully higher response rates than "exciting opportunity at a growing company!" Sourcing at volume tempts recruiters to skip that step; a constrained prompt lets you personalize quickly without inventing details about a candidate you don't actually know.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have the candidate's public profile (LinkedIn or similar) open and 2-3 real details noted — a specific project, a role change, a skill or achievement they've listed.
steps: Note 2-3 real, specific details from the candidate's public profile.
Add the role you're sourcing for and why this candidate's background is relevant to it.
Use the outreach prompt below, which bans invented candidate details and generic openers.
Ask for two variants — a first-touch message and a shorter follow-up in case there's no reply.
Check both against the candidate's actual profile before sending.
Send from your own recruiting platform or email account.
lessons.prompt:
Write a sourcing outreach message to a passive candidate. Use only the real details I give you — do not invent anything about their background, skills, or experience.

Candidate's real, relevant details (from their public profile): [PASTE 2-3 REAL DETAILS]
Role I'm sourcing for: [TITLE, brief description]
Why their background is relevant: [ONE SENTENCE]
What makes this role worth their time (be specific, not generic): [1-2 SENTENCES]

Rules:
- Open with a specific, genuine reference to one real detail from their background — not "I came across your impressive profile."
- Do not use "exciting opportunity," "growing company," or similar generic phrases without a specific detail attached.
- Be transparent that this is a recruiting outreach message, not a vague "let's connect."
- Keep it under 100 words.
- One clear, low-friction next step (e.g., a short call, a reply if interested) — not multiple asks.

Write:
1. The first-touch message.
2. A shorter follow-up (under 50 words) to use if there's no reply after about a week.
lessons.explanation: Requiring the opener to reference a specific real detail, rather than a generic compliment about their "impressive profile," is the single biggest driver of reply rates from passive candidates who've seen every generic version already. Being explicit that the message should transparently state it's recruiting outreach avoids the vague "let's connect" approach that candidates find evasive once they realize what it actually is. Keeping the ask singular and the message short respects that a passive candidate isn't looking for a new role and needs a low-effort reason to engage.
lessons.example:
Details: candidate led a migration project mentioned on their profile, recently moved from an IC to a team-lead role. Sourcing for: a senior engineering role with people-management scope. Relevance: their recent lead experience plus the migration project's technical depth.

Expected output: a message opening with something like "Saw you led the [project type] migration and recently moved into a team-lead role" rather than a generic greeting, stating plainly this is recruiting outreach for a specific role, and closing with a single low-effort ask like a reply if they're open to a short call — with a shorter, distinct follow-up version for a non-reply.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, pick one real candidate profile you're sourcing and draft both message versions with this prompt before sending through your recruiting platform.
lessons.expectedResult: A specific, transparent outreach message and a distinct follow-up, both under the word limits, with every personalized detail traceable to the candidate's actual public profile.
commonMistakes: Letting the opener default to a generic compliment when the real detail feels thin or hard to phrase.
Being vague about the fact that this is recruiting outreach, which reads as evasive once the candidate figures it out.
Sending the same message structure to every candidate for a role, which starts to feel templated even with different names swapped in.
Including multiple asks (call, resume, referral) in a single first-touch message.
lessons.proTip: Note the specific detail you used to personalize each message in your ATS or tracker — it's what makes the follow-up message feel like a continuation of the same conversation instead of a second cold open.

lessons.title: Screen CVs against role criteria fairly with Claude
lessons.summary: Get a structured, criteria-based CV screening summary with explicit bias guardrails — the AI produces a comparison against your stated must-haves, and a human makes every accept or reject decision.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured, criteria-based summary of how a CV matches your stated role requirements, built with explicit bias guardrails, used strictly as a triage aid rather than an automated accept/reject decision.
lessons.whyItMatters: CV screening is high-volume and high-risk at the same time: it's the step where unconscious bias around names, schools, employment gaps, or age-coded graduation years most easily creeps into hiring, and it's also exactly the kind of repetitive task AI is well suited to speeding up. The two facts don't cancel out — used carelessly, AI screening can encode and scale bias faster than a human ever could; used with real guardrails and a hard rule that a human makes every decision, it can make screening faster and more consistent. This lesson is about building that second version, not the first.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Write down your role's real must-have and nice-to-have criteria before you screen a single CV — deciding criteria after looking at candidates is itself a bias risk, since criteria tend to drift toward whoever you've already seen.
steps: Write your must-have and nice-to-have criteria for the role before reviewing any CVs, so criteria aren't influenced by candidates you've already seen.
Use the screening prompt below on one CV at a time, pasting only job-relevant content.
Review the output as a structured comparison, never as a pass/fail verdict — the model should say "matches / partial match / does not match / insufficient information" per criterion, not "reject."
Treat "insufficient information" flags as a signal to ask the candidate directly, not to assume the worst.
Make the actual advance/pass decision yourself, using the summary as one input alongside your own judgment.
Periodically spot-check a sample of the AI's summaries against your own independent read of the same CVs to catch drift.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me screen a CV against role criteria. This is a triage aid only — you are not making a hiring decision, and I will not use your output as an automatic accept or reject.

Role: [TITLE]
Must-have criteria: [LIST]
Nice-to-have criteria: [LIST]
CV content: [PASTE CV TEXT — role-relevant content only]

Rules:
- Evaluate only against the listed criteria. Do not factor in the candidate's name, presumed gender, age, nationality, photo, graduation year (beyond confirming a stated qualification), employment gaps (unless directly relevant to a stated criterion), or school prestige beyond whether a required degree is present.
- For each criterion, state one of: "Matches," "Partial match," "Does not match," or "Insufficient information" — never a single overall pass/fail verdict.
- Where you mark "insufficient information," say exactly what's missing rather than assuming it's absent.
- Quote or closely paraphrase the CV's own language as evidence for each rating.
- End with this exact note: "This is a structured comparison to support human review, not a hiring recommendation. A human should make the final screening decision, especially for any 'insufficient information' or 'partial match' result."
lessons.explanation: Naming the specific factors to exclude — name, presumed gender, age signals, employment gaps, school prestige — is far more effective than a general "be unbiased" instruction, because these are precisely the signals a model (like a human reviewer) will otherwise weight even when not explicitly asked to. Forcing a per-criterion rating instead of one overall verdict keeps the tool in triage mode: a recruiter reading "partial match" on one criterion has to make an actual judgment call, whereas a single pass/fail invites rubber-stamping. The required closing disclaimer isn't decoration — it's a standing reminder, attached to every single screening output, that a human owns the decision, which matters most for exactly the borderline cases where it would be easiest to defer to the AI's summary instead.
lessons.example:
Role: mid-level project manager. Must-haves: 3+ years leading cross-functional projects, experience with a named PM methodology. CV shows 4 years of project coordination experience but doesn't explicitly name a PM methodology.

Expected output: "Cross-functional project experience: Matches — CV states '4 years coordinating cross-functional launches across engineering and marketing.' PM methodology: Insufficient information — CV does not mention a specific methodology; worth asking directly rather than assuming absence." No mention of the candidate's name, graduation year, or any gap in the CV unless directly tied to a stated criterion, and the closing disclaimer present verbatim.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, write real criteria for a role you're currently hiring for, then run 3-5 real CVs through this prompt and make your own advance/pass decision on each, using the summary as one input rather than a verdict.
lessons.expectedResult: A per-criterion, evidence-quoted comparison for each CV with no factors outside your stated criteria influencing the rating, and a clear human decision made on top of — not replaced by — the summary.
commonMistakes: Treating "does not match" as an automatic rejection instead of a starting point for your own review.
Writing criteria loosely enough that "partial match" ratings pile up without clear guidance on how to resolve them.
Setting criteria after glancing at a few strong candidates, letting the bar drift toward whoever you've already seen.
Never spot-checking the AI's summaries against your own independent read, so drift or errors go uncaught.
lessons.proTip: Route every "insufficient information" result into a short clarifying question to the candidate before deciding anything — it's usually faster than guessing and it's the fairest option for a candidate whose CV simply didn't spell something out.

lessons.title: Draft HR policy and process documentation with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn policy decisions and process notes into clear, employee-facing documentation, with legal or jurisdiction-specific claims flagged for review rather than invented.
lessons.goal: Produce clear, employee-facing HR policy or process documentation from real policy decisions, with no invented legal or compliance claims and clear flags for anything that needs legal review.
lessons.whyItMatters: Policy documents — remote work, PTO, expense, leave — carry real weight: employees rely on them, and inconsistent or legally incorrect wording creates exposure the company will have to deal with later. AI is genuinely useful for turning a set of decisions into clear, consistent, well-organized language, but it must never be the source of a legal or compliance claim (what leave law requires, what's mandated in a given jurisdiction) — that has to come from the company's own confirmed decisions or actual legal guidance, with the document flagging anywhere that's still needed.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have the actual policy decisions already made (by HR leadership, legal, or founders) — this lesson turns decisions into clear documentation, it doesn't make the underlying policy decisions for you.
steps: Gather the real policy decisions and any process steps that go with them.
Use the policy documentation prompt below, which restricts content to your stated decisions.
Review the "Needs legal/compliance review" section for anything that touches jurisdiction-specific requirements.
Check that the tone matches how your company actually communicates with employees.
Route anything flagged for legal review to your actual legal counsel or compliance resource before publishing.
Publish only the reviewed, approved version, and note the effective date.
lessons.prompt:
Draft employee-facing HR policy documentation from the decisions below. Use only what I state — do not invent legal requirements, compliance claims, or jurisdiction-specific rules (e.g., what a specific state or country's leave law requires).

Policy topic: [e.g., remote work, PTO, expense reimbursement]
Our actual policy decisions: [PASTE DECISIONS, e.g., "employees may work remote up to 3 days/week, manager approval required, must be reachable during core hours 10am-3pm local time"]
Process steps involved: [PASTE, e.g., how to request, who approves, what system to use]
Audience: [e.g., all employees / a specific team]

Rules:
- Write in plain, clear language an employee can act on without follow-up questions.
- Do not state or imply any legal requirement, entitlement, or compliance obligation unless I've explicitly told you it's confirmed.
- If the policy would typically need to address something jurisdiction-specific (e.g., statutory leave minimums, overtime rules) and I haven't given you that detail, list it separately under "Needs legal/compliance review" rather than writing generic legal-sounding language into the policy itself.
- Include a clear "how to request/use this" process section using only the steps I provided.
- End with an effective-date placeholder: [EFFECTIVE DATE].
lessons.explanation: Banning invented legal or compliance language is the core guardrail for any HR policy document — a model asked to write a leave policy will otherwise happily produce plausible-sounding legal phrasing that may not match your actual jurisdiction's requirements, which is a real liability if an employee relies on it. Routing anything jurisdiction-specific into a separate "needs legal/compliance review" list, instead of writing around it with vague language, makes the gap visible to whoever reviews the draft rather than silently smoothing it over. Requiring a concrete process section keeps the document actually usable — a policy an employee can't act on without asking HR to clarify it has mostly failed at its job.
lessons.example:
Topic: remote work policy. Decisions: up to 3 remote days per week, manager approval required, must be reachable 10am-3pm local time, no mention of any state-specific requirement. Process: request via the HR system, manager approves within 2 business days.

Expected output: a plain-language policy stating the 3-day limit, approval requirement, and core-hours rule; a process section describing the HR-system request and 2-day approval window; a "Needs legal/compliance review" note flagging that jurisdiction-specific remote-work tax or labor requirements weren't addressed and should be checked before publishing, rather than the document inventing generic compliance language to fill that gap.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, take one real policy your company has actually decided on and draft the employee-facing documentation with this prompt, then route the flagged review items to your actual legal or compliance resource before publishing anything.
lessons.expectedResult: A clear, plain-language policy document with a usable process section, and an honest, separate list of anything that still needs legal or compliance sign-off before it's published.
commonMistakes: Publishing the draft without routing the flagged legal-review items to an actual legal or compliance resource.
Letting generic-sounding legal language slip into the policy body instead of the flagged section.
Documenting a process that doesn't match what actually happens operationally, causing confusion when employees follow it.
Skipping the effective-date field, leaving ambiguity about when the policy actually applies.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running "needs legal/compliance review" backlog across all your policy documents rather than resolving it document by document — it's usually more efficient for legal counsel to review several flagged items in one pass.

lessons.title: Design a structured hiring workflow with AI at each safe step with Claude
lessons.summary: Map your end-to-end hiring process and decide exactly where AI safely speeds things up and where every decision must stay human, then build a reusable Claude Project around the safe steps.
lessons.goal: Produce an explicit map of a full hiring workflow — sourcing through offer — marking which steps AI can safely assist and which must remain entirely human-decided, backed by a reusable Claude Project for the safe steps.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without a deliberate workflow, teams tend toward one of two failure modes: avoiding AI everywhere out of caution and losing real time savings, or applying it inconsistently — including at points like automated CV rejection that create real bias and compliance risk. The fix isn't a blanket rule in either direction; it's mapping the actual hiring process step by step and being explicit about where AI drafts or summarizes to speed up a human decision, versus where it must not be anywhere near the decision itself. This lesson builds that map once, then turns the safe steps into a reusable project so the speed gain is real and repeatable.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your actual hiring process stages listed (e.g., JD approval, sourcing, screening, phone screen, panel interview, decision, offer) — this works best mapped against your real process, not a generic template.
steps: List every stage of your real hiring process from requisition to offer.
For each stage, use the workflow prompt below to classify it as AI-assisted-drafting (human decides), AI-assisted-summary (human decides), or human-only — and to state why.
Pay particular attention to any stage involving candidate advancement or rejection — these should never be classified as AI-decided.
Review the classifications against your own judgment and your legal/compliance obligations; adjust anything that feels wrong for your context.
For each AI-assisted stage, write one standing prompt template (using the guardrail patterns from earlier lessons in this path).
Set up a Claude Project containing the workflow map and the standing prompt templates as project knowledge.
Review the map with your team or legal/compliance contact before rolling it out, and revisit it whenever your process changes.
lessons.prompt:
Help me classify each stage of our hiring workflow by where AI can safely assist versus where the step must stay fully human-decided.

Our hiring stages, in order: [LIST YOUR REAL STAGES, e.g., requisition approval, job description drafting, sourcing/outreach, CV screening, phone screen, panel interview, hiring decision, offer, onboarding kickoff]

For each stage, classify it as one of:
- "AI-assisted drafting" — AI can help produce a draft (message, document, summary) that a human reviews and finalizes.
- "AI-assisted summary/triage" — AI can help organize or summarize information to support a human decision, but must never issue the decision itself.
- "Human-only" — AI should not be involved in this step at all.

Rules:
- Any stage where a candidate is advanced, screened out, or where an offer/rejection decision is made must be classified as "AI-assisted summary/triage" at most — never as a stage where AI decides.
- For each stage, give a one-sentence reason for the classification.
- Flag any stage where using AI would need legal or compliance sign-off first (e.g., anything touching protected-characteristic risk or jurisdiction-specific requirements), even if you classify it as AI-assisted.

Then, for each "AI-assisted" stage, draft a short standing prompt template I could reuse for that stage, including the guardrail that a human makes the final call.
lessons.explanation: Forcing a three-way classification — rather than a simple yes/no on whether AI is allowed at a stage — is what makes the map actually usable, since most hiring stages aren't cleanly automatable or off-limits; they're places where AI can draft or summarize while a human still decides. The hard rule that any advancement or rejection decision can be "AI-assisted summary/triage" at most, never AI-decided, is the workflow-level version of the guardrail built in the CV-screening lesson, applied consistently across the whole process instead of just one step. Generating a reusable prompt template per AI-assisted stage is what turns this from a one-time planning exercise into something the team actually keeps using.
lessons.example:
Stages: JD drafting, sourcing outreach, CV screening, phone screen, panel interview, hiring decision, offer letter.

Expected output: JD drafting and sourcing outreach classified as "AI-assisted drafting" (human reviews and sends); CV screening classified as "AI-assisted summary/triage" with an explicit note that a human makes every advance/reject call; phone screen and panel interview classified "human-only" for the live conversation itself (though question-set prep is a separate, earlier AI-assisted step); hiring decision and offer approval classified "human-only"; offer letter drafting classified "AI-assisted drafting." Each with a one-sentence reason, and a reusable prompt template for each AI-assisted stage.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, map your team's actual hiring stages using this prompt, review the classifications with a colleague or your legal/compliance contact, then set up a Claude Project containing the finalized map and templates.
lessons.expectedResult: A stage-by-stage hiring workflow map with clear, defensible classifications, standing prompt templates for every AI-assisted stage, and an explicit rule — reviewed by your team — that no candidate advancement or rejection decision is ever made by AI alone.
commonMistakes: Classifying CV screening or interview scoring as fully AI-decided instead of AI-assisted-with-human-decision.
Building the workflow map once and never revisiting it as the actual hiring process changes.
Skipping legal/compliance review for stages that touch protected-characteristic or jurisdiction-specific risk.
Treating "human-only" stages as a place AI can still quietly help in the background without anyone reviewing that choice.
lessons.proTip: Put the finalized workflow map somewhere every interviewer and hiring manager can see it, not just recruiting — most inconsistent AI use in hiring comes from people outside the recruiting team who never saw the guardrails in the first place.
